text:
Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

text:
સત્તાના શિખરે બેઠેલા શાસકોને બંધારણીય મૂલ્યો, સામાજિક ન્યાય અને સત્યનો અવાજ ક્યારેય પચતો નથી. દેશના સળગતા અને સંવેદનશીલ મુદ્દાઓ પર સતત નિડરતાથી અવાજ ઉઠાવનાર સામાજિક-રાજકીય વિશ્લેષક જ્યોત્સ્ના આહિરનું ફેસબુક એકાઉન્ટ 9 ઓક્ટોબર 2026ના રોજ કેન્દ્ર સરકારના સીધા આદેશથી મેટા (Meta) દ્વારા ભારતમાં જીઓ-બ્લોક (Geo-block) કરી દેવામાં આવ્યું છે.

જ્યોત્સ્ના આહિરને મેટા તરફથી મળેલી નોટિસમાં સ્પષ્ટ જણાવાયું છે કે ભારત સરકારના આઈટી મંત્રાલય (MeitY) દ્વારા ભારતીય આઈટી રૂલ્સ ૨૦૨૧ (IT Rules 2021) અને આઈટી એક્ટની કલમ ૬૯-એ (Section 69A) હેઠળ વારંવાર કાયદાકીય રિક્વેસ્ટ મોકલવામાં આવી હતી. કાયદાકીય મજબૂરીના કારણે મેટાએ આ એકાઉન્ટ ભારતમાં અદ્રશ્ય કરવું પડ્યું છે. નોટિસમાં વપરાયેલા "Repeatedly" (વારંવાર) અને "Informed you" જેવા શબ્દો જ બતાવે છે કે સરકારને જે કન્ટેન્ટથી પેટમાં દુખાવા ઉપડતા હતા, તેને દબાવવા અગાઉ પણ અનેક પ્રયાસો થયા હતા. સૌથી શરમજનક બાબત એ છે કે આ કાર્યવાહી કરતા પહેલા યુઝરને પોતાની સફાઈ આપવાની કે સ્પષ્ટતા કરવાની એક પણ તક આપવામાં આવી નથી. આ કોઈ કાયદાકીય પ્રક્રિયા નથી પરંતુ સરકારનું સીધેસીધું તાનાશાહી અને મનસ્વી પગલું છે.

વાસ્તવમાં દિલ્હીના જંતરમંતર ખાતે ૧૦ ઓક્ટોબર ૨૦૨૬થી શરૂ થઈ રહેલા આંદોલનથી ગભરાઈને સરકારે જ્યોત્સ્ના આહિરના અવાજને કચડી નાખવા માટે જ આ પ્રતિબંધ લાદ્યો છે. જ્યોત્સ્ના આહિરનું કન્ટેન્ટ ક્યારેય પણ રાષ્ટ્રીય સુરક્ષા, જાહેર સુલેહ-શાંતિ કે દેશની એકતાને નુકસાન પહોંચાડનારું હોતું નથી. તેઓ હંમેશા બંધારણ, અનામત, ખેડૂત આંદોલન, ધાર્મિક-રાજકીય અંધશ્રદ્ધા અને અવાજહીન લોકોના હક માટે અવાજ ઉઠાવતા રહ્યા છે. પરંતુ વર્તમાન શાસકોની નજરમાં વડાપ્રધાન કે સરકારની આકરી આલોચના કરવી એ જ સૌથી મોટો ગુનો બની ગયો છે.

દેશમાં લોકશાહીનો કેવો કરુણ અંજામ આવ્યો છે તેનો આ જીવંત પુરાવો છે. સત્તાધારી પક્ષના નેતાઓ કે સમર્થકો ખુલ્લેઆમ "ગો** મારો..." જેવા ઝેરીલા અને ભડકાઉ ભાષણો આપે ત્યારે આઈટી મંત્રાલય મૌન ધારણ કરી લે છે. પરંતુ જ્યારે કોઈ નાગરિક બંધારણના દાયરામાં રહીને સરકારની નીતિઓની પોલ ખોલે, ત્યારે આઈટી કાયદાઓનો દુરુપયોગ કરીને તેનો અવાજ બંધ કરી દેવાય છે. જ્યારે સત્તા પર બેઠેલા લોકો લોકશાહીના મૂલ્યો ભૂલીને કાયદાનો દુરુપયોગ કરવા લાગે, ત્યારે વિરોધના અવાજોને દાબવા માટે આવી જ હલકી યુક્તિઓ અજમાવવામાં આવે છે. આ બ્લોકિંગ માત્ર ભારત પૂરતું સીમિત છે અને VPN દ્વારા આજે પણ આ એકાઉન્ટ જોઈ શકાય છે, પરંતુ સરકારનું આ પગલું ભારતીય લોકશાહી અને અભિવ્યક્તિની સ્વતંત્રતા પર લાગેલો એક કાળો ધબ્બો છે.

Bitchat has disappeared from Apple’s App Store and Google Play in India, while its website is also inaccessible through several Indian internet providers.

In a notice from Apple that Dorsey posted on X, India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued the demand under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, the country’s primary legal provision for government-ordered online blocking: https://t.co/2uYjZ1TbuL

The reason this matters:

Bitchat doesn’t need the internet.

It uses Bluetooth mesh networking to let nearby phones exchange encrypted messages without:

→ Cellular networks→ Internet access
→ Centralized servers

That makes it particularly useful during internet shutdowns.  And Indians noticed.

During protests in July, India accounted for roughly 85% of Bitchat’s global downloads over one week, according to Sensor Tower.

Now the restrictions come as India is seeing another wave of protests, with internet services recently suspended around parts of New Delhi.

The bigger story here isnt another app-store takedown.

Its what happens when decentralized communication tools are specifically designed to keep working when governments switch the internet off.

Statement on MeitY's notice to WhatsApp over the "usernames" feature

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has sent WhatsApp a notice about the usernames feature it announced on 29 June 2026. The notice asks the company to explain, within three days, why regulatory action should not be taken against it "for launching a feature that may increase cybercrimes", and it directs the company "not to roll out this feature until the consultation on this point is achieved to the satisfaction of the Government". The Internet Freedom Foundation is concerned that the notice has no clear basis in law. It is an attempt by the executive to decide what a company may build and ship, which no statute permits.

The notice treats the launch of a lawful feature as a wrong the company must justify. That reverses the ordinary position especially given the absence of any clear legal power that exists. MeitY does not name any provision that lets it approve a product feature before release or order one withdrawn, because there is none, and the provisions it does cite do not supply that power.

Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 is a safe harbour that protects an intermediary from liability for what its users post, so long as it observes due diligence. It decides when a platform can be held liable. It is not a power for MeitY to decide what features the platform may offer. Sections 66C and 66D punish identity theft and cheating by personation. They are criminal offences, tried by courts, aimed at the person who steals an identity, not at the maker of a tool that a third party misuses. Also, on MeitY's logic, a telecom operator could be told not to sell SIM cards because SIM cards are used in almost every online fraud. 

Rule 3(1)(b), Rule 3(2) and Rule 4 of the IT Rules, 2021 are due diligence and grievance obligations and cannot be converted into a licensing scheme. Section 69A, the one provision that lets MeitY control what appears online, permits the blocking of specific information through a set procedure. It says nothing about which features a company may build. Further the IT Rules, 2021 are subordinate legislation made under Sections 79 and 87 of the IT Act, and subordinate rules cannot travel beyond the parent statute (Ajoy Kumar Banerjee v. Union of India). If a rule cannot exceed the Act, a letter certainly cannot. The power to require prior permission for a feature is not in the Act, not in the Rules, and cannot be created by a notice. 

MeitY has tried this before. In March 2024 it told the same large intermediaries, among them AI Companies, to obtain its explicit permission before deploying under-tested AI models. That was criticised as an overreach that sought to build a licensing mechanism with no empowering provision in the IT Act, and within a fortnight MeitY withdrew it and dropped the permission requirement. This notice repeats the move for a single feature and goes further, because it names one company, sets a three-day clock, and bars the launch until MeitY is satisfied. 

This matters beyond WhatsApp. A power asserted against one company by letter can be turned on any company and any feature. On this reasoning MeitY could tell a browser not to switch on a privacy setting by default, or a payments app not to add a login method, each time until it was content. The notice also invokes traceability, through Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 and the identification of the "first originator" of a message. Rule 4(2) has been challenged as exceeding its parent provision and resting on no law made by Parliament, and that challenge is pending before the Delhi High Court. Raising it against a feature meant to share fewer identifiers fits a pattern. 

We ask MeitY to state the exact provision of law under which this notice, and the direction to halt the roll-out, has been issued, and to withdraw that direction. It should stop using Section 79 and the contested traceability rule as leverage to control product design and to reverse features that improve privacy. Impersonation and fraud are real risks, but they are met by enforcing the criminal law against those who commit them, and by open processes that rest on identified legal powers. They are not met by MeitY deciding, in private and by letter, what features Indians may use. That is a licence raj for software features.

New Delhi, 1 July 2026

IFF Statement: Blocking of the Cockroach Janta Party's Instagram account

July 22, 2026

The Instagram account of the Cockroach Janta Party (@cockroachjantaparty) is no longer accessible to users in India. Meta's notice states only that it complied with "a legal request to restrict this content". No order has been published and the legal basis, the issuing authority, and the reasons remain unknown.

We emphasise that the account is primarily engaged in acts of political speech that enjoy the full protection of Article 19(1)(a). The account has been restricted after the movement's march to Parliament over the NEET paper leak, and while the Delhi High Court examines allegations of excessive police force against protesters. Viewed in this background the blocking of its social media account at this moment is the suppression of dissent.

The secrecy compounds the illegality. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A of the IT Act on the strength of its procedural safeguards. In Anuradha Bhasin, it held that orders restricting fundamental rights must be published. These safeguards are defeated when the originator learns of a blocking action from an error message.

We also note that Meta's notice refers to a "legal request", not an order.  We call on MeitY to disclose the order, furnish a copy to the account holder, and provide a hearing. We call on Meta to inform the account holder of the specific legal process it received. Wholesale blocking of an entire account is disproportionate and unconstitutional.

Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

text:
More click bait bullshit:

The video is real footage of Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz signing a bill, but the post’s claim that he legalized terminating healthy newborns is false. What changed is narrower and still disputed.
The clip shows Walz at a table signing legislation while a group of women behind him smile and clap. It is from the May 2023 signing of SF 2995, the large omnibus health and human services bill (Chapter 70). That bill contained many abortion-related changes; the viral edit focuses on the atmosphere at the ceremony and ties it to the born-alive language. The same footage has circulated in political posts since the 2024 vice-presidential debate.
What the law actually did
Before 2023, Minnesota’s Born Alive Infants Protection Act (2015 updates to a 1976 statute) said a born-alive infant resulting from an abortion “shall be fully recognized as a human person” and that medical personnel must take “all reasonable measures consistent with good medical practice… to preserve the life and health of the born alive infant.” It also required reporting of such cases to the Department of Health and included civil and licensing penalties.
SF 2995, which Walz signed, rewrote that provision. The current text still says an infant born alive “shall be fully recognized as a human person, and accorded immediate protection under the law,” and still requires “all reasonable measures consistent with good medical practice… to care for the infant who is born alive.” It dropped the phrases “as a result of an abortion” and “to preserve the life and health,” changed the heading from “medical care” to “care,” repealed the specific reporting requirement and the related civil-penalty language, and applied the rule to all born-alive infants rather than only abortion survivors.
House author Rep. Tina Liebling described the remaining duty, in floor debate, as comfort care rather than efforts to preserve life. The same bill also repealed Minnesota’s post-viability abortion limit, waiting-period and informed-consent rules, and other abortion restrictions.
Reported cases before the change
While reporting was still required, the Minnesota Department of Health recorded:
•2019: 3 infants born alive during abortion procedures; none survived (one pre-viable, one with anomalies, one given comfort care).
•2021: 5 such infants; none survived (two pre-viable, two given comfort care, one with anomalies).
•None reported in 2020 or 2022.
Those figures are in the department’s induced-abortion reports and were confirmed by outlets including The Dispatch. After 2023 the specific born-alive reporting mandate was gone, so later comparable public counts do not exist.
How the two sides read it
Pro-life groups such as Minnesota Citizens Concerned for Life argue the rewrite removed a guarantee of lifesaving measures and left only “care,” which the sponsor called comfort care, while also eliminating the data and penalties that made non-treatment visible. They say viable infants or infants with disabilities are the ones most affected.
Fact-checks from Snopes and PolitiFact say the bill did not authorize killing born infants. Homicide laws still apply to any person born alive; the statute still requires reasonable measures consistent with good medical practice; and the wording change was presented by supporters as ending a requirement for futile interventions on non-viable infants. Walz has said claims that the law lets doctors withhold care from abortion survivors misstate what he signed.
The accurate middle ground is that the 2023 law weakened and generalized the earlier specific duty to preserve life and health, removed reporting and dedicated penalties, and was defended by its author as comfort-care language—while leaving intact the recognition of a born-alive infant as a person protected by ordinary criminal law. It did not create a legal right to terminate a healthy newborn.

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

France 24. BBC. Reuters. Al Jazeera. Washington DC. Human Rights Watch.

When does a government stop calling it foreign interference and start asking, why is the entire world saying the same thing about us?

Here is what is actually happening inside India right now:

▪️ India has the world’s strictest content takedown window; just 3 hours. No major democracy, and no major authoritarian regime, moves this fast against its own citizens’ speech.

▪️ Under the new IT Rules 2026 amendment, it’s not just news outlets being targeted. Ordinary users, influencers, and anyone who simply shares a news post can now fall under the government’s content blocking framework.

▪️ The Internet Freedom Foundation has formally called this “digital authoritarianism” and a “dangerous expansion of executive power.” These are not opposition politicians, these are constitutional lawyers and digital rights experts.

▪️ Since 2014, India’s government takedown orders have surged 14 times; from 201 to 14,775. And post 2022, this data was denied under RTI on grounds of national security.

▪️ Meta alone was forced to restrict 28,000+ pieces of content in India in just the first six months of 2025; following government orders.

▪️ India currently ranks 151 out of 180 in the World Press Freedom Index. We are sitting between countries most Indians would be ashamed to be compared with.

▪️ The Supreme Court’s own Shreya Singhal judgment; a landmark free speech ruling, is being systematically bypassed by these rules. 

This is not policy. This is contempt of constitutional precedent.

The government will say this is about deepfakes. About national security. About public order.

But when 138 YouTube videos were taken down for allegedly defaming Adani, a private businessman, it stopped being about security a long time ago.

France 24 is not attacking India. France 24 is holding up a mirror.

The question is, why is this government so terrified of what Indians might see in it?

Why RMG can restart after the 10 Feb 2026 IT Rules amendment — and why it still hasn’t (yet). A legal breakdown:

The 10 Feb 2026 amendment to the IT Rules did not repeal or dilute the PROGA 2025 Act.
What it did was introduce a conditional statutory exception — not an automatic revival.

1️⃣ The baseline position: PROGA 2025's criminal prohibition

Under Section 5, PROGA 2025:
“No person shall offer, aid, abet, induce or otherwise engage in the offering of any online money game or online money gaming service.”

Violation attracts Section 9 penalties:

➡️ up to 3 years’ imprisonment and/or ₹1 crore fine.
This prohibition became effective from the date of Presidential assent (22 Aug 2025) — no rule-making required.

2️⃣ Why payments stopped — and why they matter:

Under Section 7, PROGA 2025:
“No bank, financial institution or payment intermediary shall engage in, permit, aid or facilitate any transaction towards payment for any online money gaming service.”
This made UPI, cards, wallets and gateways criminally exposed if they processed RMG transactions.
Hence the immediate, industry-wide payment freeze.

3️⃣ What the 10 Feb 2026 IT Rules amendment actually changed:

The amendment introduced the concept of a “permissible online real-money game” under the IT Rules framework.
Crucially, it says:

- A real-money game is not prohibited only if it is
• verified as permissible
• certified by a government-recognised Self-Regulatory Organisation (SRO)
• compliant with prescribed safeguards.
This is an exception clause — not a repeal.

4️⃣ How this legally unlocks PROGA (if conditions are met)
Once a game is certified as “permissible” under the IT Rules:

It falls outside the definition of a prohibited “online money game”
(A) Section 5 PROGA no longer applies to that game,
(B) Section 7 payment ban no longer triggers
(C) Advertising restrictions tied to “online money games” also lift for that specific certified game
(D) No certification = PROGA ban continues in full force.

5️⃣ Why RMG hasn’t restarted at scale despite the amendment:

Because, as of now:
- SRO recognition is limited / evolving
- Certification is game-specific, not platform-wide
- Any misclassification risks criminal prosecution, not just regulatory fines
- Platforms will not operate on “interpretation” when jail liability exists.

6️⃣ Most important legal shift (often missed):

Earlier:
Courts decided skill vs chance post-facto.
Now:
Statutory gatekeeping precedes operation.
No SRO approval → no legality → no payments.

7️⃣ Bottom line:

The Feb 10, 2026 amendment did not “revive” RMG.
It created a narrow, conditional doorway.

RMG can restart only game-by-game, only after SRO certification, and only within IT Rules safeguards.

Until then, PROGA’s criminal prohibitions remain fully operative.
Law changed — but risk calculus didn’t.

#PROGA2025 #OnlineGamingLaw #RMG #ITRules2026 #LegalAnalysis #GamingRegulationIndia

Hi Creators!

ASK ME QUESTIONS REGARDING X RULES ON POSTING YOUR CONTENT.

I WILL ANSWER THEN WITH PLEASURE.

Here’s one hypothetical question that intrigues every creator’s mind.

And the answer follows.

Q: Does X take it as violation of rules if posts created by AI or Grok are posted on the platform?

A: No. Posting content created by AI, including Grok, is not itself a violation of X’s rules.

X’s rules focus on deception, harm, spam, and certain restricted categories—not on whether a person or a model wrote or generated the post.

What the rules actually say:

Under the Authenticity policy, synthetic or manipulated media is restricted only when it is shared deceptively and is likely to cause harm (for example, widespread confusion on public issues, public-safety risk, or serious harm). 

That includes media of a real person fabricated or simulated with AI. Sharing the same kind of media in a non-deceptive way is allowed. X may also label synthetic media so people can see the context.
Ordinary AI-written text, images, or video—jokes, commentary, art, summaries, fictional scenes, and similar posts—does not violate the rules just because AI made them.

Narrower limits that do apply: 

•Creator Revenue Sharing (announced March 2026): unlabeled AI-generated videos of armed conflict can get a creator suspended from the revenue program for 90 days, and permanently on a repeat. That is a monetization penalty, not a general ban on AI posts.

•Spam and platform manipulation still apply. Bulk, duplicative, or automated posting that manipulates reach or trends can be enforced whether a human or an AI wrote it. Developer rules also require prior approval for AI-powered automated reply bots.

•Fake personas that use AI-generated profile photos or bios to deceive others are not allowed.

•AI-generated child sexual exploitation material is prohibited, as is non-consensual intimate imagery (including synthetic). Consensual adult AI content is allowed if it is labeled like other adult content.

•In India, under the IT Rules Amendment 2026, users must declare synthetically generated information that looks real and label it prominently. X says it watermarks images and videos generated or edited by Grok.

So a normal post drafted or illustrated by Grok is fine. Problems arise only if the post is spam, impersonation, unlabeled misleading media that can cause harm, or another existing rule violation.

text:
Against the Digital Writs of Assistance A Response to the President's Cyber Strategy Dedicated to the thirty-third anniversary of A Cypherpunk's Manifesto by Eric Hughes, published March 9, 1993. By Jeffrey Wernick
The principle is simple.
You do not go behind someone's back to obtain information about them without their permission. If the government wants to know something about you, it must ask you directly, or it must obtain a warrant from a neutral judge who agrees the need is real. That standard should be high. The exception should be rare. And the person whose information is sought should know it is being sought.
Everything else in this essay is an elaboration of that principle, or a description of how thoroughly the Trump administration is violating it.

If you already know that going behind someone's back is wrong, and you do, because every human being raised in any culture that has a concept of trust knows this, then you already understand the constitutional crisis now underway. You do not need a law degree. Your moral intuition is correct. The elaborate legal architecture built around surveillance is largely an apparatus for managing exceptions to a principle that should have very few exceptions.
The Fourth Amendment did not invent this principle. It recognized it. The founders understood that a government which could search without cause, without notice, and without limit was not a government that served its citizens. It was a government that owned them.
Consider what would not have existed in a world with the surveillance architecture the Trump administration is now building.
The Federalist Papers were published anonymously. Hamilton, Madison, and Jay signed them "Publius," choosing anonymity to ensure their arguments were judged on merit rather than on the authority or vulnerability of their authors.
Their opponents wrote under pseudonyms too. "Brutus," whose Anti-Federalist essays remain among the most penetrating critiques of centralized power ever written in America, was almost certainly Robert Yates, a New York judge who said so under a name that protected him while his argument circulated. None of them signed their real names. All of them shaped the republic.

Thomas Paine published Common Sense anonymously in January 1776. He knew what attribution meant in a world where speech could be punished. He chose to let the argument travel without a target attached to it.
Benjamin Franklin spent decades writing under pseudonyms. Silence Dogood. Poor Richard. Franklin understood that anonymity was not evasion. It was access. It allowed a writer to say true things without calculating the personal cost of every sentence.
Now consider what a government with DOGE's database, Palantir's analytical infrastructure, and the Trump cyber strategy's architecture of real-time network surveillance would have done with any of this.
Publius's identity would have been discovered within hours. Brutus would have been identified and exposed before his third essay. Thomas Paine would have been traced to his printer before Common Sense had time to circulate. The pseudonymous debate that produced the Bill of Rights, in which Americans argued fiercely and freely about what kind of government they were willing to accept, would have been visible to the government being debated.
You cannot have that debate under surveillance. You cannot argue freely against power when power is watching every argument you make and storing it in a database for later use.
This is not hypothetical. It is the logic of the system being built. The administration's own executive order mandated that its data apparatus be used to identify people who speak up against the administration. A government that considers political dissent a data category to be tracked is not a government that would have tolerated Publius.
The Federalist Papers could not have been written under a government that surveils all communication in real time and maintains a database connecting the identities of every citizen to everything they have ever written, sent, or searched.
The republic those papers argued for could not have been founded under those conditions.
What is being built now is not compatible with how this country was created.
That, too, is self-evident.
In 1761, James Otis stood in a Boston courtroom and challenged the writs of assistance, general authorizations that allowed British customs officials to search any home, any business, any private space, without naming the person, without specifying what they sought, without any requirement of suspicion. Go everywhere. Look at everything. Take what is useful.
John Adams later wrote that when Otis spoke, "then and there the child Independence was born."
George Mason drew the same lesson. He refused to sign the Constitution without a Bill of Rights, warning that without explicit written protections, the new federal government would accumulate powers capable of overwhelming the liberties of the people. Mason did not trust good intentions. He trusted structure.

James Madison agreed. He wrote in Federalist No. 51 that if men were angels, no government would be necessary. Because they are not, power must be restrained by design, not by disposition. The structure must supply the defect of better motives.
Thomas Jefferson stated the trajectory plainly. The natural progress of things, he wrote, is for liberty to yield and government to gain ground.
The Fourth Amendment was the answer. Particular warrants, not general ones. A named person. A named place. A named object. A neutral magistrate who had to agree the cause was just.
Information about a person belongs to that person. The government must justify taking it. The justification must be specific. Someone independent must agree.
A century and a half later, technology changed the instruments of intrusion but not the principle.
Justice Louis Brandeis, in his dissent in Olmstead v. United States in 1928, warned that new methods of surveillance would allow the government to observe private life in ways unimaginable to the framers. The Constitution protects what he called the right to be let alone. He also issued the warning that has proved most prophetic. The greatest dangers to liberty lurk in insidious encroachment by men of zeal, well-meaning but without understanding. The threat was not malice. It was the sincerity of people convinced that their cause justified the method.
Justice William O. Douglas carried that warning forward. The tools themselves make pervasive observation easy, and what is easy becomes tempting, and what is tempting becomes routine.

Justice Robert H. Jackson, who had prosecuted the architects of Nazi tyranny at Nuremberg, stated it most starkly. Uncontrolled search and seizure is one of the first and most effective weapons in the arsenal of every arbitrary government.
They were describing the architecture. Not the intention. The intention can change with every election. The architecture persists.
It was precisely this that the cypherpunks recognized when the internet was young and the choices about its architecture were still open.
Eric Hughes wrote thirty-three years ago today that privacy is necessary for an open society. His argument was moral, not technical. Privacy is the power to decide what you reveal about yourself, and to whom, and when. Destroy it and every other freedom becomes conditional on the good intentions of whoever holds the data. Good intentions are not a constitutional standard. Hughes was translating the Fourth Amendment into mathematics. Cypherpunks write code.
Timothy May extended the argument. Mathematics does not obey political authority. You cannot rely on promises. You need structural guarantees. In the digital age, those guarantees come from cryptography.

Now consider what the Trump administration has built.
DOGE, operating under an executive order granting it "full and prompt access to all unclassified agency records, software systems, and IT systems," moved through the federal government's most sensitive databases without asking anyone's permission. Social Security records. Tax filings. Medicaid enrollment. Immigration files. Food assistance data. Housing records. State voter rolls.
A separate executive order mandated "unfettered access" to data from all state programs receiving federal funding, including data held by third parties.

The Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board was gutted the moment it was most needed. Its chairperson and two members were dismissed in January 2025, leaving it unable to function at precisely the moment its function was most required.
Palantir was engaged to build the infrastructure connecting these streams. Oracle deepened its strategic partnership with Palantir and embedded itself further across federal government systems. Together with DOGE, these companies form the private architecture of a surveillance apparatus that privacy experts and scholars at Harvard and Brookings have described as the most comprehensive civilian data consolidation project in American peacetime history.
The Social Security Administration later reported that DOGE employees had secretly and improperly shared sensitive personal data, circumvented IT rules to move records to outside servers, and that the agency still cannot account for what was taken or where it went.
Not one of the people whose data moved through these systems was asked. Not one was notified. Not one warrant was obtained. Not one magistrate reviewed the cause.
Going behind everyone's back. At federal scale. In real time.
The Trump cyber strategy, released March 7, 2026, promises to "counter the spread of the surveillance state and authoritarian technologies that monitor and repress citizens."
The administration wrote those words while constructing the surveillance architecture just described.
This is not irony. It is instruction. Power names the danger in order to claim ownership of the resistance to it.

The strategy calls for real-time surveillance of networks and a deregulatory framework that converts private communications infrastructure into an instrument of national observation. It is five pages long. The Biden administration's comparable strategy ran thirty-five pages. The brevity is not modesty. It is a promissory note.
In March 2025, senior administration officials including the National Security Advisor, the Secretary of Defense, the Vice President, and the Director of the CIA conducted sensitive military planning on Signal, accidentally including the editor of The Atlantic in the discussion. The officials responsible for building a surveillance architecture to monitor the communications of every American were themselves using end-to-end encrypted private messaging to shield their own deliberations from oversight.
Privacy for those who hold power. Surveillance for everyone else.
Now consider who is building the infrastructure and what they have said about it.
Larry Ellison, co-founder of Oracle, Trump donor, and a central figure in the Stargate artificial intelligence infrastructure project, described his vision at an Oracle financial analysts meeting. Police body cameras, car cameras, doorbell cameras, security cameras, and drones would stream continuously to Oracle data centers where artificial intelligence would monitor the feeds in real time. "Citizens will be on their best behavior because we are constantly recording and reporting everything that's going on." He said this as a feature, not a warning.
Ellison went further at the World Governments Summit in Dubai. "We need to unify all the national data," including genomic data. Constant surveillance, he added, would make for a happier citizenry.

Benjamin Franklin already answered this.
Franklin is already in this essay. He is the man who published as Silence Dogood and Poor Richard for decades, who chose anonymity as the precondition of honest speech.
That same Franklin wrote the sentence that stands as the most precise response to Ellison's offer. Those who would give up essential liberty to purchase a little temporary safety deserve neither liberty nor safety.
Franklin was not making a policy argument. He was issuing a moral verdict. The transaction Ellison proposes — surrender your privacy, your anonymity, your freedom from observation, and in return you will be safe and happy — is the transaction Franklin condemned. Not as unwise. As a forfeiture.
The man who wrote the liberty-safety aphorism and the man who wrote as Poor Richard are the same man making the same argument from two directions. Anonymity is the condition that makes free thought possible. Trading it for safety destroys the thing it claims to protect.
The word Ellison chose was happier. Not freer. Not more sovereign. Happier. A content subject and a free citizen are not the same thing.
Now the same logic is being extended from physical space into digital space, and from the executive branch into the legislature.
Twelve bipartisan bills are currently moving through Congress under the banner of child safety. Each one would require identity verification to access the internet. The SCREEN Act would mandate age verification for any website Congress decides is harmful to minors. Other proposals push the requirement to the operating system level, meaning a person would have to prove their identity before their device could connect to the internet at all.
The justification is always children. The mechanism always produces the same result. A person's offline identity is permanently linked to their online behavior. Every site visited. Every search conducted. Every article read. Every opinion expressed. All of it attached to a name, an address, a government-issued document number.

Who bears the greatest risk? Not the children the bills claim to protect. Trans people in states with hostile legislatures. Undocumented immigrants. Women seeking reproductive healthcare across state lines. Whistleblowers. Journalists. Activists. There is no mechanism that verifies a child's identity without first verifying every adult's.
What these bills propose is that no one, ever again, may do what Franklin, Madison, Hamilton, Jay, Paine, and Yates did. Every word published on the internet would be linked to a verified identity. The infrastructure of pseudonymous democratic argument, the infrastructure on which the republic was founded, would be permanently dismantled.
This is the Franklin bargain offered twice in the same political moment. Ellison offers it for physical space. Congress offers it for digital space. Franklin already answered both. The transaction is a forfeiture.
The governments of China, Russia, and Saudi Arabia already use online identity systems to track and imprison dissidents. The United Kingdom's Online Safety Act has already been used to restrict content related to Palestine. These are not warnings about hypothetical futures. They are descriptions of documented destinations.
This is what makes the current moment categorically different from every prior expansion of surveillance power in American history.
The writ of assistance required a customs officer. COINTELPRO required informants. PRISM required intercept access. Each required human labor, and human labor imposes practical limits. A surveillance system that anyone can query by typing a question and receiving an answer in seconds has no practical limit. It scales to the entire population simultaneously. It never sleeps. It never forgets.
Artificial intelligence is what makes this categorically new. A database connecting every American's tax records, medical history, location data, financial transactions, communications, and internet activity becomes something qualitatively different when a language model can query it in plain English in real time.

Once built, this architecture is extraordinarily difficult to dismantle. It belongs to every future administration of either party. The founders wrote permanent limits because they knew that temporary abuses have a way of becoming permanent architecture.
There is a final self-defeating irony that belongs in the record.
The Salt Typhoon intrusion, in which Chinese state-sponsored hackers compromised at least nine American telecommunications companies, succeeded in part by exploiting the lawful intercept systems — the government-mandated backdoors — that American law had required those companies to build for authorized surveillance. The back door installed for domestic law enforcement was the door foreign adversaries walked through.
Building more surveillance infrastructure does not make the country safer. It creates more targets. A centralized database connecting every American's records is the single most valuable target in the world for any hostile intelligence service that wishes to own it. Mandate identity verification for internet access and you have created a master key to the online identity of every American citizen, stored somewhere, accessible to whoever can reach it.

The same structure that protects the citizen from the government protects the citizen from everyone who wants what the government has accumulated.
The complications are not accidental.
When the principle is simple, power builds complexity around it. Third-party doctrine. Statutory exceptions. National security carve-outs. Regulatory frameworks calibrated to permit what the plain principle prohibits. This is the weapon.  The complexity that makes ordinary citizens feel unqualified to object to what they correctly know is wrong.
The third-party doctrine holds that when you voluntarily share information with another party, you lose your Fourth Amendment protection in that information. You told your bank your account balance. You told your phone company who you called. You told your doctor your diagnosis. Because you told someone else, the government can obtain it without a warrant.

The founders would not have recognized this as law. They would have recognized it as the writ of assistance wearing a suit.
When you disclose your tax information to the IRS, your location to your phone carrier, your food purchases to your bank, you are not consenting to government surveillance. You are participating in modern life. The third-party doctrine converts that participation into a permanent waiver of your privacy rights. It is converting necessity into consent and consent into forfeiture.
This is the legal machinery that makes DOGE possible. Every database they accessed was assembled from third-party disclosures. Every record they merged was information someone shared with an institution under legal frameworks that promised separation. The third-party doctrine is the reason no warrant was required. It is how the general warrant was laundered into legality.
The Supreme Court began questioning it in Carpenter v. United States in 2018, with Chief Justice Roberts writing that the Court must ensure preservation of that degree of privacy against government that existed when the Fourth Amendment was adopted. The Carpenter decision was a crack in the doctrine. What the Trump administration is building is a system designed to operate in the space that crack has not yet opened wide enough to close.
Jefferson called certain truths self-evident because they were available to any honest person willing to look directly at them. You do not need to understand the doctrine to know that combining your tax records, your medical history, your location data, and your immigration status without your knowledge is a betrayal of the terms under which you disclosed each of them.
Somewhere in Texas, a woman crossed a state line for a procedure legal where she was going. Somewhere in Phoenix, a man attended a protest and found his name in a database assembled from records he had provided, separately and in good faith, to institutions that promised to keep them separate. Neither of them consented. Neither of them was warned. Neither of them had a magistrate review the cause.
They are the people Otis was arguing for in 1761. Their situation is not complicated. It is a general warrant. It is arbitrary power. It is the government going behind their backs.
The Fourth Amendment was written so this would not happen.

What does a constitutional cyber strategy look like?
The government defends infrastructure and pursues genuine foreign threats with specific cause, judicial oversight, and accountability to someone outside the chain of command.
The executive orders eliminating data silos should be rescinded. Cross-agency data sharing requires statutory authority, congressional approval, and judicial review. The Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board should be restored. CISA should be rebuilt. Encryption should be strengthened. The internet ID verification proposals should be rejected on First and Fourth Amendment grounds. The Palantir and Oracle contracts should be submitted to full public and congressional review. Any proposal to build a centralized national database combining the records of every American should be treated as what it is, the writ of assistance at computational scale.

None of this is complicated. All of it follows from the principle.
Mason said write it down. Madison said structure the power. Brandeis said watch the technology. Douglas said watch the temptation. Jackson said remember what happens when governments stop watching themselves. Hughes said use the mathematics. May said the mathematics will hold if citizens choose to use it.
They were all saying the same thing.
You do not go behind someone's back.

Not without asking. Not without a warrant. Not without cause so specific and a judge so independent that the exception proves the rule rather than consuming it.
That is the American standard. It was self-evident to the people who built this republic.
The Federalist Papers could not have been written under the surveillance architecture being built today. Common Sense could not have circulated. Poor Richard could not have published. Brutus could not have warned us. The founders could not have founded.
What is being built now is not compatible with how this country was created.
And that should be self-evident too.

Sources: White House Cyber Strategy for America (March 7, 2026); Trump National Security Strategy (November 2025); McIntyre v. Ohio Elections Commission (1995); Olmstead v. United States, Brandeis dissent (1928); Carpenter v. United States (2018); Federalist No. 51 (Madison); NPR, ACLU, Brookings Institution, Harvard Kennedy School, Center for American Progress on DOGE data access; Larry Ellison, Oracle Financial Analyst Meeting (September 2024) and World Governments Summit, Dubai (February 2025); The Atlantic, Signalgate reporting (March 2025); SCREEN Act (H.R. 1623, S. 737, 119th Congress); Kids Online Safety Act (119th Congress); Electronic Frontier Foundation and National Coalition Against Censorship on internet ID verification proposals; Eric Hughes, A Cypherpunk's Manifesto (1993); Timothy May, The Crypto Anarchist Manifesto (1988).
