⚖️ Cannabis Rescheduling's Two Tracks

The legal challenge to cannabis rescheduling finally has a timetable. On October 9, the Justice Department and the opponents suing to undo the reform jointly proposed a briefing schedule to the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals. If the court adopts it, the case will be fully briefed by February 19, 2027, with both sides asking for oral argument “as soon as reasonably practicable” afterward and before the court’s summer recess.

For an industry used to deadlines that slide, this is something rarer: dates both sides signed.

Who Is Suing, And Over What

Three consolidated petitions are in play. One comes from Smart Approaches to Marijuana and the National Drug and Alcohol Screening Association, represented by Torridon Law, where former Attorney General William Barr is a partner. A second comes from a coalition of activists, physicians and MMJ International Holdings. The third comes from the attorneys general of Indiana and Nebraska; Louisiana has dropped out.

Their target is Attorney General Todd Blanche’s April order, which moved state-licensed medical cannabis and FDA-approved marijuana products to Schedule III immediately. The court declined to freeze that order in September, so it stays in force while the lawyers write.

The Proposed Calendar
• November 24: petitioners’ consolidated opening brief
• December 1: amicus briefs supporting petitioners
• January 13: the government’s response
• January 20: amicus briefs supporting the government
• February 5: petitioners’ reply
• February 12: joint appendix
• February 19: final briefs

The government gets the longer runway, partly because its window spans the holidays and partly because its counsel has international travel booked from November 27 to December 13. Even federal appellate litigation yields to a good itinerary.

Implication One: The Status Quo Is Locked In

A denied stay plus a February finish means the April order remains the law through at least the first quarter of 2027. Add a spring argument and the months a complex agency case usually takes to decide, and a ruling before mid-2027 looks unlikely. For medical operators, Schedule III treatment and the 280E relief that came with it will cover year-end 2026 books and probably much of 2027. The binary risk has not gone away. It has been rescheduled, which is fitting.

Implication Two: Standing Comes First

The parties asked for expanded word limits, citing “multiple standing issues.” That tells you where the first fight is. At the stay stage, DOJ argued the challengers have “pocketbook interests” in keeping marijuana in Schedule I and are not the people the Controlled Substances Act was written to protect.

If the panel agrees, the case ends without touching the merits, and the same petitioners inherit the same problem when they challenge the final rule. If the panel finds standing, opponents get a blueprint for round two. Either way, the standing ruling travels.

Implication Three: Two Tracks, One Clock

The lawsuit rides side saddle to the administrative process, which is where broad rescheduling still lives. DEA Chief Administrative Law Judge Derek Julius took testimony in June and July and received final briefs in August. The only step left was his recommendation to DEA Administrator Terrance Cole, who makes the final call.

Then, on September 29, Julius stayed the record to consider an opponents’ motion to add a Government Accountability Office report, which found DEA has no written policies for how staff evaluate and schedule substances. DEA’s response is due October 13. That is the first date on the calendar that matters, and it arrives six weeks before any appellate brief.

From There, Sequencing Drives Everything:

If Julius reopens the record, supplemental briefing pushes his recommendation later, and the court case sets the pace.

If he declines, a recommendation could land while opening briefs are still being drafted, and a final rule could follow during or shortly after briefing.

A final rule before the court rules would change the case. A rule built on a full hearing record is a sturdier vehicle than an order, and it would let the government argue that parts of the challenge have been overtaken. Opponents would file a fresh petition and try to fold it into the existing one.

A court ruling first cuts the other way. Whatever the panel says about the attorney general’s authority, or the test for “currently accepted medical use,” becomes the frame DEA has to write within.

Expect the GAO report to work both rooms. It is already before the judge, and it will almost certainly appear in the November 24 brief as evidence that the process was improvised.

Implication four: the industry is watching from the gallery

Two medical marijuana companies tried to intervene on the government’s side. The court said no, but will let them file amicus briefs, due January 20. That leaves the defense of the order entirely with DOJ.

The encouraging part is how DOJ has behaved: it opposed the stay, and it agreed to a schedule the parties call “materially shorter” than many complex agency cases. The less comfortable part is that the government’s litigation choices are not the industry’s to make.

The Wildcard

The House Appropriations Committee has voted to block further steps toward rescheduling. Bipartisan lawmakers have said they do not expect that to survive, but it is a third venue to monitor while the other two grind forward.

What To Watch

• October 13: DEA’s filing on whether to reopen the record.
• The court’s scheduling order: whether it adopts the proposal and the longer word limits.
• November 24: how much of the opening brief is standing, how much is merits, and how the GAO report is used.
• January 13: the government’s full defense, on paper for the first time.
• The argument date: a spring slot keeps a 2027 decision in view.

February is when the paper stops. The part that moves markets comes after.

— Anthony Varrell @V_arrell

An extract from an article by Avay Shukla relevent to today's judgement on Swatantra  Bhardwaj bail-
'Jurisprudence in India today appears to be governed by four made-in-India/swadeshi doctrines which should be a blot on any justice system: fait accompli, sealed cover, ignore the science, and reward the criminal. Importantly, even constitutional challenges to the executive’s actions are kept on the backburner for so long (Article 370, CAA, SIR, Shiv Sena split) that by the time they are decided, it is impossible to turn back the clock and undo what the government of the day has already implemented on the ground.
The sealed cover has become the standard fallback option for denying full disclosure to civil society petitioners, or for not giving rebuttable reasons for a particular judgment (Rafale, Pegasus, Vantara, Hindenburg). Increasingly, this spectre of our swadeshi jurisprudence, like the executive, shows disdain and contempt for science, as in the case of stray dogs, Aravalli mountains, the Char Dham highway, and the Great Nicobar project. More trust is reposed on government-appointed committees and patently partisan ministries than on scientists, domain experts and specialised organisations working in the relevant field. Finally, this mutant form of justice also ensures that the criminal will be duly allowed to keep the proceeds of his crime (Ram Mandir theft, electoral bonds) even as his actions are declared irregular! A judicial paraprosdokian if ever there was one.'
Avay Shukla- Bumpy swadeshi model of justice.
The Tribune 19 July 2026

Statement on MeitY's notice to WhatsApp over the "usernames" feature

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has sent WhatsApp a notice about the usernames feature it announced on 29 June 2026. The notice asks the company to explain, within three days, why regulatory action should not be taken against it "for launching a feature that may increase cybercrimes", and it directs the company "not to roll out this feature until the consultation on this point is achieved to the satisfaction of the Government". The Internet Freedom Foundation is concerned that the notice has no clear basis in law. It is an attempt by the executive to decide what a company may build and ship, which no statute permits.

The notice treats the launch of a lawful feature as a wrong the company must justify. That reverses the ordinary position especially given the absence of any clear legal power that exists. MeitY does not name any provision that lets it approve a product feature before release or order one withdrawn, because there is none, and the provisions it does cite do not supply that power.

Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 is a safe harbour that protects an intermediary from liability for what its users post, so long as it observes due diligence. It decides when a platform can be held liable. It is not a power for MeitY to decide what features the platform may offer. Sections 66C and 66D punish identity theft and cheating by personation. They are criminal offences, tried by courts, aimed at the person who steals an identity, not at the maker of a tool that a third party misuses. Also, on MeitY's logic, a telecom operator could be told not to sell SIM cards because SIM cards are used in almost every online fraud. 

Rule 3(1)(b), Rule 3(2) and Rule 4 of the IT Rules, 2021 are due diligence and grievance obligations and cannot be converted into a licensing scheme. Section 69A, the one provision that lets MeitY control what appears online, permits the blocking of specific information through a set procedure. It says nothing about which features a company may build. Further the IT Rules, 2021 are subordinate legislation made under Sections 79 and 87 of the IT Act, and subordinate rules cannot travel beyond the parent statute (Ajoy Kumar Banerjee v. Union of India). If a rule cannot exceed the Act, a letter certainly cannot. The power to require prior permission for a feature is not in the Act, not in the Rules, and cannot be created by a notice. 

MeitY has tried this before. In March 2024 it told the same large intermediaries, among them AI Companies, to obtain its explicit permission before deploying under-tested AI models. That was criticised as an overreach that sought to build a licensing mechanism with no empowering provision in the IT Act, and within a fortnight MeitY withdrew it and dropped the permission requirement. This notice repeats the move for a single feature and goes further, because it names one company, sets a three-day clock, and bars the launch until MeitY is satisfied. 

This matters beyond WhatsApp. A power asserted against one company by letter can be turned on any company and any feature. On this reasoning MeitY could tell a browser not to switch on a privacy setting by default, or a payments app not to add a login method, each time until it was content. The notice also invokes traceability, through Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 and the identification of the "first originator" of a message. Rule 4(2) has been challenged as exceeding its parent provision and resting on no law made by Parliament, and that challenge is pending before the Delhi High Court. Raising it against a feature meant to share fewer identifiers fits a pattern. 

We ask MeitY to state the exact provision of law under which this notice, and the direction to halt the roll-out, has been issued, and to withdraw that direction. It should stop using Section 79 and the contested traceability rule as leverage to control product design and to reverse features that improve privacy. Impersonation and fraud are real risks, but they are met by enforcing the criminal law against those who commit them, and by open processes that rest on identified legal powers. They are not met by MeitY deciding, in private and by letter, what features Indians may use. That is a licence raj for software features.

New Delhi, 1 July 2026

The 11th National Annual Stakeholders’ Consultation named “A Decade of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015: Progress, Challenges and Priorities for the Next Decade” was held on October 10–11 at the Supreme Court Auditorium, New Delhi, organised by the Supreme Court of India, UNICEF India and the Union Ministry of Women and Child Development. 

Odisha was represented by Dr. Mrinalini Darswal, IAS, Commissioner-Cum-Secretary Women & Child Development Dept. 

The consultation brought together judicial experts, senior officials and child rights stakeholders to discuss progress and priorities in child protection and juvenile justice.

Odisha showcased its achievements in implementing the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, re-affirming its commitment to child-centred care, protection, rehabilitation and empowerment.

Key achievements include:
🔹 Family-Based Care: Sponsorship support increased from 689 children in 2016 to 5,550 in 2026, while children in Child Care Institutions declined from 17,411 to 7,289.
🔹 Support for Vulnerable Children: Initiatives such as Ashirbad, Jashoda and Kalika provide financial assistance, long-term support and safe childcare.
🔹 Empowerment: Education, life skills, vocational training, sports and cultural activities help children build confidence and prepare for independent futures.
🔹 Child-Friendly Justice: Improved infrastructure, judicial oversight, rescue and restoration initiatives, and digital safety programmes strengthen child protection systems.

Speaking at the consultation, Dr. Mrinalini Darswal, IAS, Commissioner-cum-Secretary, Department of Women & Child Development, Government of Odisha, emphasised:

“Institutional care remains necessary for children who need it, but it should not become the default. Our systems increasingly aim to support children safely within families and communities wherever possible.”

Odisha’s experience highlights that effective child protection requires strong families and communities, rehabilitation and opportunities for every child to thrive.
Every child deserves a family, protection, and a future filled with dignity, opportunity and hope.

କିଶୋର ନ୍ୟାୟ ଅଧିନିୟମ, ୨୦୧୫ର ଏକ ଦଶନ୍ଧି: ପ୍ରଗତି, ଆହ୍ୱାନ ଏବଂ ଆଗାମୀ ଦଶନ୍ଧି ପାଇଁ ପ୍ରାଥମିକତା ନାମରେ    ୧୧ତମ ଜାତୀୟ ବାର୍ଷିକ ଅଂଶୀଦାର ସମ୍ମିଳନୀ, ଅକ୍ଟୋବର ୧୦-୧୧ ତାରିଖରେ ନୂଆଦିଲ୍ଲୀର ସୁପ୍ରିମକୋର୍ଟ ଅଡିଟୋରିୟମରେ ଅନୁଷ୍ଠିତ ହୋଇଥିଲା। ଏହାକୁ ଭାରତର ସୁପ୍ରିମକୋର୍ଟ, ୟୁନିସେଫ୍ ଇଣ୍ଡିଆ ଏବଂ କେନ୍ଦ୍ର ମହିଳା ଓ ଶିଶୁ ବିକାଶ ମନ୍ତ୍ରଣାଳୟ ମିଳିତଭାବେ ଆୟୋଜନ କରିଥିଲେ । 

ଓଡ଼ିଶା ପ୍ରତିନିଧି ଭାବରେ ମହିଳା ଓ ଶିଶୁ ବିକାଶ ବିଭାଗର କମିଶନର-ତଥା-ସଚିବ ଡ. ମୃଣାଳିନୀ ଦର୍ଶୱାଲ, ଆଇ.ଏ.ଏସ୍. ଅଂଶଗ୍ରହଣ କରିଥିଲେ। ଏହି ସମ୍ମିଳନୀରେ ଶିଶୁ ସୁରକ୍ଷା ଏବଂ କିଶୋର ନ୍ୟାୟ କ୍ଷେତ୍ରରେ ପ୍ରଗତି ଏବଂ ପ୍ରାଥମିକତା ଉପରେ ଆଲୋଚନା କରିବା ପାଇଁ ନ୍ୟାୟିକ ବିଶେଷଜ୍ଞ, ବରିଷ୍ଠ ଅଧିକାରୀ ଏବଂ ଶିଶୁ ଅଧିକାର ଅଂଶୀଦାରମାନେ ଏକତ୍ରିତ ହୋଇଥିଲେ। କିଶୋର ନ୍ୟାୟ (ଶିଶୁମାନଙ୍କର ଯତ୍ନ ଏବଂ ସୁରକ୍ଷା) ଅଧିନିୟମ, ୨୦୧୫ କାର୍ଯ୍ୟକାରୀ କରିବାରେ ଓଡ଼ିଶା ନିଜର ସଫଳତା ପ୍ରଦର୍ଶନ କରିଥିଲା ଏବଂ ଶିଶୁ-କୈନ୍ଦ୍ରିକ ଯତ୍ନ, ସୁରକ୍ଷା, ପୁନର୍ବାସ ଏବଂ ସଶକ୍ତିକରଣ ପ୍ରତି ଏହାର ପ୍ରତିବଦ୍ଧତାକୁ ପୁନଃପ୍ରକାଶ କରିଥିଲା।

ଓଡ଼ିଶାର ପ୍ରମୁଖ ସଫଳତାଗୁଡ଼ିକ ହେଲା:
• ପାରିବାରିକ ଯତ୍ନ: ପ୍ରାୟୋଜକ ସହାୟତା ୨୦୧୬ରେ ୬୮୯ ଜଣ ଶିଶୁରୁ ବୃଦ୍ଧି ପାଇ ୨୦୨୬ରେ ୫,୫୫୦ ଜଣରେ ପହଞ୍ଚିଛି, ଯେତେବେଳେ କି ଶିଶୁ ଯତ୍ନ ଅନୁଷ୍ଠାନଗୁଡ଼ିକରେ ଥିବା ଶିଶୁଙ୍କ ସଂଖ୍ୟା ୧୭,୪୧୧ ରୁ କମି ୭,୨୮୯କୁ ଖସିଆସିଛି।
• ଅସୁରକ୍ଷିତ ଶିଶୁମାନଙ୍କୁ ସହାୟତା: 'ଆଶୀର୍ବାଦ', 'ଯଶୋଦା' ଏବଂ 'କଳିକା' ଭଳି ପଦକ୍ଷେପଗୁଡ଼ିକ ଆର୍ଥିକ ସହାୟତା, ଦୀର୍ଘକାଳୀନ ସହଯୋଗ ଏବଂ ନିରାପଦ ଶିଶୁ ଯତ୍ନ ପ୍ରଦାନ କରୁଛି।
• ସଶକ୍ତିକରଣ: ଶିକ୍ଷା, ଜୀବନ କୌଶଳ, ବୃତ୍ତିଗତ ପ୍ରଶିକ୍ଷଣ, କ୍ରୀଡ଼ା ଏବଂ ସାଂସ୍କୃତିକ କାର୍ଯ୍ୟକ୍ରମଗୁଡ଼ିକ ଶିଶୁମାନଙ୍କୁ ଆତ୍ମବିଶ୍ୱାସ ବଢ଼ାଇବା ଏବଂ ସ୍ୱାଧୀନ ଭବିଷ୍ୟତ ପାଇଁ ପ୍ରସ୍ତୁତ ହେବାରେ ସାହାଯ୍ୟ କରୁଛି।
• ଶିଶୁ-ଅନୁକୂଳ ନ୍ୟାୟ: ଉନ୍ନତ ଭିତ୍ତିଭୂମି, ଆଇନଗତ ତଦାରଖ, ଉଦ୍ଧାର ଓ ପୁନରୁଦ୍ଧାର ପଦକ୍ଷେପ ଏବଂ ଡିଜିଟାଲ୍ ସୁରକ୍ଷା କାର୍ଯ୍ୟକ୍ରମଗୁଡ଼ିକ ଶିଶୁ ସୁରକ୍ଷା ବ୍ୟବସ୍ଥାକୁ ମଜଭୁତ କରୁଛି।

ସମ୍ମିଳନୀରେ ମତାମତ ରଖି ଓଡ଼ିଶା ସରକାରଙ୍କ ମହିଳା ଓ ଶିଶୁ ବିକାଶ ବିଭାଗର କମିଶନର-ତଥା-ସଚିବ ଡ. ମୃଣାଳିନୀ ଦର୍ଶୱାଲ ଗୁରୁତ୍ୱାରୋପ କରି କହିଥିଲେ "ଯେଉଁ ଶିଶୁମାନଙ୍କୁ ପ୍ରକୃତରେ ଅନୁଷ୍ଠାନଗତ ଯତ୍ନ ଆବଶ୍ୟକ, ସେମାନଙ୍କ ପାଇଁ ଏହା ଜରୁରୀ ହୋଇପାରେ , କିନ୍ତୁ ଏହା ସବୁବେଳେ ପ୍ରାଥମିକ ବିକଳ୍ପ ହେବା ଉଚିତ୍ ନାହିଁ। ଆମର ଶିଶୁ ସୁରକ୍ଷା ବ୍ୟବସ୍ଥାଗୁଡ଼ିକ କ୍ରମଶଃ ଏହି ଦିଗରେ କାର୍ଯ୍ୟ କରୁଛି ଯେଉଁଠାରେ ସମ୍ଭବ ଶିଶୁମାନେ ପରିବାର ଏବଂ ସମାଜ ମଧ୍ୟରେ ନିରାପଦରେ ରହି ସହାୟତା ପାଇପାରିବେ।"
ଓଡ଼ିଶାର ଏହି ଅନୁଭୂତି ପ୍ରମାଣ କରେ ଯେ ପ୍ରଭାବଶାଳୀ ଶିଶୁ ସୁରକ୍ଷା ପାଇଁ ଦୃଢ଼ ପରିବାର ଓ ସମାଜ, ପୁନର୍ବାସ ଏବଂ ପ୍ରତ୍ୟେକ ଶିଶୁର ବିକାଶ ପାଇଁ ସୁଯୋଗ ଏକାନ୍ତ ଆବଶ୍ୟକ ।
ପ୍ରତ୍ୟେକ ଶିଶୁ ଏକ ପରିବାର, ସୁରକ୍ଷା ଏବଂ ମର୍ଯ୍ୟାଦା, ସୁଯୋଗ ଓ ଆଶାରେ ଭରପୂର ଏକ ଭବିଷ୍ୟତ ପାଇବାକୁ ଯୋଗ୍ୟ।

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

Statement on MeitY's notice to WhatsApp over the "usernames" feature

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has sent WhatsApp a notice about the usernames feature it announced on 29 June 2026. The notice asks the company to explain, within three days, why regulatory action should not be taken against it "for launching a feature that may increase cybercrimes", and it directs the company "not to roll out this feature until the consultation on this point is achieved to the satisfaction of the Government". The Internet Freedom Foundation is concerned that the notice has no clear basis in law. It is an attempt by the executive to decide what a company may build and ship, which no statute permits.

The notice treats the launch of a lawful feature as a wrong the company must justify. That reverses the ordinary position especially given the absence of any clear legal power that exists. MeitY does not name any provision that lets it approve a product feature before release or order one withdrawn, because there is none, and the provisions it does cite do not supply that power.

Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 is a safe harbour that protects an intermediary from liability for what its users post, so long as it observes due diligence. It decides when a platform can be held liable. It is not a power for MeitY to decide what features the platform may offer. Sections 66C and 66D punish identity theft and cheating by personation. They are criminal offences, tried by courts, aimed at the person who steals an identity, not at the maker of a tool that a third party misuses. Also, on MeitY's logic, a telecom operator could be told not to sell SIM cards because SIM cards are used in almost every online fraud. 

Rule 3(1)(b), Rule 3(2) and Rule 4 of the IT Rules, 2021 are due diligence and grievance obligations and cannot be converted into a licensing scheme. Section 69A, the one provision that lets MeitY control what appears online, permits the blocking of specific information through a set procedure. It says nothing about which features a company may build. Further the IT Rules, 2021 are subordinate legislation made under Sections 79 and 87 of the IT Act, and subordinate rules cannot travel beyond the parent statute (Ajoy Kumar Banerjee v. Union of India). If a rule cannot exceed the Act, a letter certainly cannot. The power to require prior permission for a feature is not in the Act, not in the Rules, and cannot be created by a notice. 

MeitY has tried this before. In March 2024 it told the same large intermediaries, among them AI Companies, to obtain its explicit permission before deploying under-tested AI models. That was criticised as an overreach that sought to build a licensing mechanism with no empowering provision in the IT Act, and within a fortnight MeitY withdrew it and dropped the permission requirement. This notice repeats the move for a single feature and goes further, because it names one company, sets a three-day clock, and bars the launch until MeitY is satisfied. 

This matters beyond WhatsApp. A power asserted against one company by letter can be turned on any company and any feature. On this reasoning MeitY could tell a browser not to switch on a privacy setting by default, or a payments app not to add a login method, each time until it was content. The notice also invokes traceability, through Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 and the identification of the "first originator" of a message. Rule 4(2) has been challenged as exceeding its parent provision and resting on no law made by Parliament, and that challenge is pending before the Delhi High Court. Raising it against a feature meant to share fewer identifiers fits a pattern. 

We ask MeitY to state the exact provision of law under which this notice, and the direction to halt the roll-out, has been issued, and to withdraw that direction. It should stop using Section 79 and the contested traceability rule as leverage to control product design and to reverse features that improve privacy. Impersonation and fraud are real risks, but they are met by enforcing the criminal law against those who commit them, and by open processes that rest on identified legal powers. They are not met by MeitY deciding, in private and by letter, what features Indians may use. That is a licence raj for software features.

New Delhi, 1 July 2026

A guy was about to tap "Buy Now" on a $299.99 espresso machine on Amazon. Full price.

His wife, a former Amazon fulfillment operations lead, took the phone out of his hands.

She scrolled 3 inches down the exact same product page. Tapped one small gray link. Same machine. Same brand. Same model. Shipped from the same Amazon warehouse. $164.19.

"How?"

"Look at the fulfillment tag. See where it says Amazon Resale: Like New? That means the outer cardboard box got dented on a delivery pallet. The $299.99 is the standard retail listing. The $164.19 is the exact same unopened machine inside a bruised box. Same return protection. Same two-day Prime truck. $135 difference. Because you only look at the yellow Buy Now button."

He looked at her.

"How long have you known this?"

"Since my first week at the fulfillment center. 5 years ago. Everything on Amazon runs on warehouse codes and pricing triggers. LPN stickers track returns. The 15th of the month forces sellers into liquidation. A simple URL code unlocks hidden 70% clearance. I've been using them for years. You've been paying retail for years."

Here's every hidden Amazon warehouse code and pricing rule and what it means for your wallet:

Code 1: "Used - Like New" under Amazon Resale. Brand new products trapped in dented cardboard at up to 40% off retail.

She said this is the single biggest pricing loophole on the entire platform, because most shoppers see the word "Used" and immediately scroll past it.

"Right below the yellow 'Buy Now' button on millions of items, there is a small box that says 'Save with Used - Like New' sold by Amazon Resale, formerly called Amazon Warehouse. Most buyers assume someone used the product at home and sent it back dirty. In the vast majority of cases for 'Like New' grade, that's completely false."

"Inside an Amazon fulfillment center, strict platform compliance rules dictate what can be sold as 'New.' If a forklift bumps a pallet and crushes the corner of a cardboard box, that item is dead as 'New' inventory. If a customer orders the wrong color, opens the outer shipping tape, sees their mistake, and drops it at UPS without ever touching the product inside, it cannot go back into the 'New' bin."

"Instead, a warehouse associate runs a quick visual grading check, sees the factory plastic seal is still intact, grades it 'Used - Like New,' and the pricing system automatically slashes the price by 25% to 50% to clear the shelf space."

"She said 'Used - Like New' and 'Used - Very Good' are how employees furnish their entire homes. 'When I worked the grading station, I watched brand-new $400 kitchen appliances, Sony headphones, and power tools get marked down by $150 simply because the cardboard box had a tear from a box cutter. The machine inside had never been plugged into a wall. Shoppers who click the yellow button pay an extra $135 just to have unwrinkled cardboard that they throw in the recycling bin ten minutes after delivery.'"

Code 2: The "LPN" Barcode Sticker. The warehouse License Plate Number that gives you instant leverage when a "New" item isn't new.

She said this three-letter code is printed on a small white sticker on millions of packages, and knowing what it means gives you immediate leverage with customer support.

"Every single item that passes through an Amazon return center gets slapped with a white barcode sticker starting with the letters 'LPN,' which stands for License Plate Number. That sticker ties the physical box to a specific return ID in Amazon's internal database, recording the return history of that exact unit."

"Here is why you need to check every box you order: fulfillment center workers move fast under intense hourly quotas. Mistakes happen constantly. A returned item with an LPN sticker occasionally gets routed back into the 'New' inventory bin by mistake."

"If you pay full retail price for a 'New' item and it arrives with a white LPN barcode sticker stuck over the original manufacturer barcode, you did not receive untouched factory inventory. You paid full price for a previously returned unit."

"When this happens, you don't have to pack it up and drive to UPS. Open the Amazon customer chat and use the exact warehouse terminology. Tell the agent: 'I paid full retail price for a New item, but the package arrived with an LPN return sticker on the box. Since I received previously returned inventory, I would like an open-box partial credit adjustment to keep it instead of returning it.'"

"She said mentioning the LPN code changes the chat conversation immediately. 'The moment you point out the LPN sticker, the support rep knows a fulfillment grading error happened. Because it costs Amazon money to ship that item back and re-grade it, support agents can offer a partial refund or promotional credit on the spot so you keep the item without triggering a return.'"

In the repair and restoration units of the "West" group of forces, military repair specialists restore combat tracked and wheeled vehicles around the clock. In addition to fixing breakdowns, military personnel are equipping the vehicles with dynamic and anti-drone protection kits. As repairmen note, they do not experience a shortage of spare parts and specialized tools. On the contrary, the warehouses always have the required volume.

Also, constant interaction with representatives of military equipment manufacturing plants has been established. It happens that specific crews and calculations contact repair and restoration units with private, specific requests to modify, make changes to their tank, infantry fighting vehicle or launcher. In order to continuously repair and restore tanks, heavy tracked vehicles and other combat equipment delivered from the front line, specialists quickly set up equipment repair and restoration points.

Specialists paid special attention to issues of maintenance and repair of military equipment of troops operating at a significant distance from temporary deployment and stationing points. Thanks to the high professionalism of the servicemen of the repair units, as well as technical equipment, repairmen carry out restoration work of any complexity in the field.

The military personnel perform their tasks in several shifts, which allows work to be carried out around the clock. After repairs, they take the crew's places and check each vehicle before returning it to the front. The vehicle arrives at the site, where the serviceability of the units and assemblies is checked. Near the repair shop, there is a special testing ground for this, where combat vehicles are checked in various modes over rough terrain.

∆∆ What the Supreme Court cannot do?
√√ It cannot remove, suspend, or formally censure the CEC as a disciplinary or punitive action.
Formal removal of the CEC is exclusively a parliamentary process under Article 324(5) of the Constitution (same manner and grounds as a Supreme Court judge: proved misbehaviour or incapacity, requiring a special majority in both Houses after inquiry under the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968).
In short, the Supreme Court acts as a constitutional check on the exercise of power by the Election Commission. It does not have the authority to impose a formal censure on the CEC personally. Any call for removal must go through Parliament.
No, the Supreme Court cannot formally “censure” the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) in the sense of imposing a disciplinary reprimand or sanction that affects his tenure.

∆∆ What the Supreme Court can do
√√ The Court has the power of judicial review over the actions and decisions of the Election Commission of India (ECI) under Article 324 and related laws. In practice, this means it can:
Examine whether decisions of the ECI (including those attributed to the CEC) are legal, constitutional, or taken in accordance with the prescribed procedure (for example, collectively by the multi-member Commission rather than unilaterally).
Issue directions, interim orders, or injunct (bar/restrain) specific decisions if they are found irregular or contrary to law.
Make strong critical observations or remarks in its judgments or during hearings about the functioning of the Commission or the CEC.
Potentially initiate or entertain contempt proceedings if its own orders are violated (though Section 16 of the 2023 CEC and Other Election Commissioners Act grants broad immunity from civil and criminal proceedings for official acts, which has itself been debated in court).
In recent hearings related to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and allegations of unilateral decision-making, the Supreme Court has issued notices to the ECI, refused interim orders suspending the CEC, and indicated that if statutory requirements (such as collective decision-making) are not followed, it can injunct those decisions. It has stressed that it is examining institutional compliance rather than pursuing individual removal. @grok

NEW DELHI, INDIA - The fight has moved beyond a dispute over one official. By treating the CEC as part of a larger chain of political responsibility, Rahul Gandhi is attempting to shift public attention from administrative decisions to the structure of power behind them.

The Tandav comparison serves a practical purpose. It frames the protests as an open-ended movement rather than a campaign tied to a single march, court filing or deadline. That makes it harder to measure success or failure through any one event.

Pressure on election institutions has become a recurring feature of Indian politics, but opposition criticism is now increasingly directed at the legitimacy of institutional decisions rather than specific election outcomes. That raises the political cost of every future ruling made by the commission.

The immediate argument is about accountability. The larger contest is over whether public trust in election management can be separated from the wider political battle surrounding it. The office remains in place, but its authority has become part of the dispute itself.

Starlink just told India it's ready to launch, pending final government approvals. Here's what you need to know.

Lauren Dreyer, SpaceX's Vice President of Starlink Business Operations, spoke at India Mobile Congress in New Delhi today. It also says it can help accelerate efforts to connect India 100%.

The remaining step is government authorisation. Under the DoT's current authorisation terms, satellite communication operators must also pay an annual licence fee of 8% of AGR.

Reaction is split. Some investors see India as a huge market for Starlink. Some critics want it banned, citing security fears.

- Hundreds of antennas installed

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

IFF condemns journalist’s detention and the seizure of their phones during the Delhi protests

New Delhi, 12 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the detention of journalists and the seizure of their' phones by the Delhi Police during the protests of 10 and 11 October 2026. The protests, sought the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. According to a report in Newslaundry, the police took three official phones from its reporters and an intern on 10 October. BOOM lost contact with its reporter Jagriti Trisha after her phone was taken, and Indian Express Hindi said its journalist Siya's phone was snatched on 11 October. Scroll's Shoaib Daniyal says he was pressured to delete videos he recorded inside a police bus.

Section 106 of the BNSS allows the police to seize property only in connection with a suspected offence, and Section 105 requires every seizure to be video recorded and the recording sent to a Magistrate. No provision, seizure memo or recording has been made public, and it is not known whether the phones were unlocked or their data copied. A reporter's phone holds unpublished material, private messages and the identities of sources. Under K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India, (2017) 10 SCC 1, any intrusion into privacy must be backed by law, necessary and proportionate. Making a journalist delete footage of police action destroys the record of how the police used their powers.

Further, on 5 October, the Delhi Police issued "Guidelines for journalists" asking reporters to carry identity cards issued by their organisations "and/or valid PIB/DIP accreditation cards". On 10 October, Newslaundry reported that police were asking media personnel whether they were YouTubers, refusing entry to those who were, and asking for PIB accreditation. Press cards however did not prevent detention and reporters from at least nine outlets were detained on 10 October, and from at least seven on 11 October. Digital journalist Pragya Mishra was detained in the RK Ashram area, and by her account her camera person was beaten even though both carried identification.

Detentions and the use of force are not ordinarily part of IFF's work given our focus on digital rights. We address them here because they affect the freedom of speech and expression of digital first journalists, who report and publish through their phones. Here we note, Article 19(1)(a) protects the freedom of the press (Indian Express Newspapers (Bombay) Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, (1985) 1 SCC 641), whether a journalist works for a newspaper or runs a YouTube channel. PIB accreditation has never been a condition for reporting from a public place. When the police check accreditation at a protest and detain those without it, they are illegally deciding who may report.

We note that on 11 October, Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana of the Supreme Court heard a contempt petition alleging violation of the Court's order of 9 October on metro and train services, and a habeas corpus petition concerning the reported detention of about 7,000 people. The Court found a prima facie case and issued notice. Taking note of the Solicitor General's statement that internet services had been restored, it directed that that "Lawyers, journalists and other professionals shall not be hindered in discharge of their professional duties in any manner whatsoever." However, to our regret, there has been little compliance of this order as journalists were detained again that afternoon, a few hours after the order.
Our demands

We call upon the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Government of NCT of Delhi and the Delhi Police to:

1) Return every phone taken from journalists, disclose the legal basis, seizure memo and Section 105 recording for each, and confirm whether any data was copied.
2) Instruct all personnel in writing that no one may be made to delete footage or stopped from recording police action, and preserve all body-camera footage.
3) Withdraw the advisory of 5 October to the extent that it makes accreditation a condition for reporting, and ensure that journalists and creators covering protests are not detained or obstructed.
4) Place before the Supreme Court on 13 October 2026 the names of all journalists detained, the grounds of detention and the time of release. We also support the press bodies' call for an inquiry, which should be independent, time-bound and cover the complaints made by women journalists.
5) IFF will track compliance before the hearing on 13 October 2026 and is examining legal remedies, including for the phones taken from journalists. 

Journalists and creators who were detained, had devices taken, were made to delete footage, or had posts or accounts restricted for covering the protests may write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in.

IFF condemns journalist’s detention and the seizure of their phones during the Delhi protests

New Delhi, 12 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the detention of journalists and the seizure of their' phones by the Delhi Police during the protests of 10 and 11 October 2026. The protests, sought the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. According to a report in Newslaundry, the police took three official phones from its reporters and an intern on 10 October. BOOM lost contact with its reporter Jagriti Trisha after her phone was taken, and Indian Express Hindi said its journalist Siya's phone was snatched on 11 October. Scroll's Shoaib Daniyal says he was pressured to delete videos he recorded inside a police bus.

Section 106 of the BNSS allows the police to seize property only in connection with a suspected offence, and Section 105 requires every seizure to be video recorded and the recording sent to a Magistrate. No provision, seizure memo or recording has been made public, and it is not known whether the phones were unlocked or their data copied. A reporter's phone holds unpublished material, private messages and the identities of sources. Under K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India, (2017) 10 SCC 1, any intrusion into privacy must be backed by law, necessary and proportionate. Making a journalist delete footage of police action destroys the record of how the police used their powers.

Further, on 5 October, the Delhi Police issued "Guidelines for journalists" asking reporters to carry identity cards issued by their organisations "and/or valid PIB/DIP accreditation cards". On 10 October, Newslaundry reported that police were asking media personnel whether they were YouTubers, refusing entry to those who were, and asking for PIB accreditation. Press cards however did not prevent detention and reporters from at least nine outlets were detained on 10 October, and from at least seven on 11 October. Digital journalist Pragya Mishra was detained in the RK Ashram area, and by her account her camera person was beaten even though both carried identification.

Detentions and the use of force are not ordinarily part of IFF's work given our focus on digital rights. We address them here because they affect the freedom of speech and expression of digital first journalists, who report and publish through their phones. Here we note, Article 19(1)(a) protects the freedom of the press (Indian Express Newspapers (Bombay) Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, (1985) 1 SCC 641), whether a journalist works for a newspaper or runs a YouTube channel. PIB accreditation has never been a condition for reporting from a public place. When the police check accreditation at a protest and detain those without it, they are illegally deciding who may report.

We note that on 11 October, Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana of the Supreme Court heard a contempt petition alleging violation of the Court's order of 9 October on metro and train services, and a habeas corpus petition concerning the reported detention of about 7,000 people. The Court found a prima facie case and issued notice. Taking note of the Solicitor General's statement that internet services had been restored, it directed that that "Lawyers, journalists and other professionals shall not be hindered in discharge of their professional duties in any manner whatsoever." However, to our regret, there has been little compliance of this order as journalists were detained again that afternoon, a few hours after the order.
Our demands

We call upon the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Government of NCT of Delhi and the Delhi Police to:

1) Return every phone taken from journalists, disclose the legal basis, seizure memo and Section 105 recording for each, and confirm whether any data was copied.
2) Instruct all personnel in writing that no one may be made to delete footage or stopped from recording police action, and preserve all body-camera footage.
3) Withdraw the advisory of 5 October to the extent that it makes accreditation a condition for reporting, and ensure that journalists and creators covering protests are not detained or obstructed.
4) Place before the Supreme Court on 13 October 2026 the names of all journalists detained, the grounds of detention and the time of release. We also support the press bodies' call for an inquiry, which should be independent, time-bound and cover the complaints made by women journalists.
5) IFF will track compliance before the hearing on 13 October 2026 and is examining legal remedies, including for the phones taken from journalists. 

Journalists and creators who were detained, had devices taken, were made to delete footage, or had posts or accounts restricted for covering the protests may write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in.

In Brazil, the Supreme Court ordered X to block named accounts and appoint a legal representative. Musk refused, published sealed orders, and shut the office. X was banned for over a month. Starlink told regulators it would not block X. Justice Moraes then froze Starlink’s Brazilian accounts and took about $3.3 million to cover X’s fines, treating both firms as one group under Musk. Starlink complied once its licence was at risk. X later blocked the accounts, paid the fines, and named a representative. The ban was lifted in October 2024. The fortune did not matter. text:
Yesterday I got a bit roasted on X because I said my agent checks me in for my flights, so let me double down: it also helps me book basically every plane ticket.

I just landed in India and they asked for one of those crazy health/immigration forms with passport info, where you’re staying, flight details, etc. I sent it to my agent, it filled everything out, great job, I went back to reading my book.

A bunch of people replied: “I’m a competent adult, I know how to do this, I don’t need AI.”

Which is totally fair. Do whatever works for you! 

I also know how to wash dishes and I love my dishwasher. I know how to write a letter, put it in an envelope and go to the post office, and yet I prefer email. I know how to do mental arithmetic and I still use a calculator.

The point of technology is very rarely that humans are incapable of doing the thing. It’s that our time and attention are better spent somewhere else.

Instead of spending 20 minutes fighting with a PDF, finding my passport number, hotel address and flight information in five different places, I can read my book. Instead of manually replying to three emails just to send my landlord some insurance information, an agent can handle it and I get another 20 minutes with my 18-month-old daughter, Josephine.

I think people underestimate AI agents for two reasons.

First, capitalism has this amazing tendency to take things that were once reserved for rich people and, through technology and scale, give them to everyone. Rich people have had executive assistants forever. Someone books their flights and restaurants, coordinates meetings, answers routine communications, fills out paperwork, reminds them what they forgot. AI is going to give some version of that to billions of people.

Second, a huge amount of economic progress is simply removing friction. Coase would call a lot of this transaction costs. One form takes 15 minutes, one email takes 3 minutes, one reservation takes 10 minutes. None of these things individually feels revolutionary, but remove thousands of them over a lifetime and it compounds into something enormous.

So yes, I am perfectly capable of checking myself into a flight but now I just don’t see why I should.

It is beyond understanding why and how Central Government is giving so much importance to the issue when liberal approach of Central Government in sending the minister and other senior ones to opposition leaders to find some solution was later turned down by the senior opposition leaders. What India needs a politics of cordiality amongst ruling party and main opposition party like was in days when PV Narsimharao was Prime Minister and Atal Bihari Vajpayee was the Opposition Leader. What India needs is drastic and important poll-reforms to achieve the goal that trough an ordinance without waiting for some never to-be-achieved political consensus. Simultaneous elections to Lok Sabha and state-assemblies should be three-tier with elections to municipal bodies also included in the ideal system. Elections to posts of President and the Vice President may be held simultaneously by all MPs and MLAs in the manner President is elected but through EVMs equipped with VVPAT on nominations signed by at least 34-percent MPs to ensure direct elections. Prime Minister/Chief Ministers with Speakers and Deputy Speakers of the lower Houses should be elected through secret and compulsory vote of members of the Lower Houses through Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) equipped with VVPAT on nominations signed by at least 34-percent members. Such an elected Prime Minister/Chief Minister may be removed by same process but with compulsion of naming alternate leader in the same motion. Members not opting to vote may lose voting-right in the House even though retaining membership of the House. Without adopting such a system, aspect “One-Nation One-Election” can never be a dream-cum-true because of mid-term elections caused due to hung Lok Sabha/state-assembly or fall of governments in between. Even present Prime Minister, Chief Ministers, Speakers and Deputy Speakers may be re-elected on lines suggested here-above. Since a person cannot represent two constituencies or become member of both Parliament and state-assembly, no person should be allowed to contest from more than one constituency or for both Parliament and state-assembly. A sitting MP or MLA should resign first from his/her earlier seat before filing nomination for the other seat. Membership of a Parliamentarian must be auto-terminated on taking oath in a state as minister (or Chief Minister) and vice-versa to prevent situation like Atal Bihari Vajpayee government falling due to single controversial vote of the then Odisha Chief Minister Girdhar Gomango who did not resign from Lok Sabha even becomin Odisha Chief Minister. 

Secret voting for Rajya Sabha elections should be restored but through EVMs equipped with VVPAT system with simultaneous elections for full time and part time members. text:
Celebrating RTI Act on 12th October : Objective incomplete without Citizen’s Charter and Grievance Redressal Bill

There was a proposal to introduce “The Right of Citizens for Time Bound Delivery of Goods and Services and Redressal of their Grievances Bill, 2011” (The Citizen’s Charter and Grievance Redressal Bill) after implementation of “Right-To-Information Act, 2005” to fulfill the objective of providing timely redressal of Grievances to the public. But unfortunately the much-awaited and most desired bill has still not been introduced. Rather “The Citizen’s Charter and Grievance Redressal Bill” is much more necessary to achieve the desired goal. Union Government should fulfill the much-needed requirement by introducing the said bill which will make government-functionaries to solve problems of the people in an effective manner reducing over-burdened government-functionaries presently utilizing much of their time and resources Under Right-To-Information Act. Rather with quick disposal of public-grievances through “The Citizen’s Charter and Grievance Redressal Bill” will make government-functionaries working fast thus resulting in further savings of time and resources of government-departments and public authorities.

Otherwise also, a fresh look is necessary for revising RTI Rules drafted long back in the year 2012 to prevent misuse of RTI Act which will further drastically reduced time and resources of public authority spent on handling RTI matters. Ever since first amendment in RTI Act was done ever since its implementation on 12th October2005, some NGOs and opposition parties are crying that sunshine Act is diluted! But the amendment made in the year 2019 aimed to change status and tenure of Information Commissioners, in no way affected users of RTI Act. Insertion of section 44(3) in “The Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023” removing riders to section 8(1)(j) of RTI Act in fact necessary to preserve Parliamentary privilege and remove confusion through the term “public-interest”. Having a rider of “Public Interest” was not needed in view of section 8(2) of RTI Act which provides access to information in case public interest overweighs the harm protected. It is for the first time that Central Information Commission has full strength of Chief Information Commissioner and ten Information Commissioners sworn on 15.12.2025.

Otherwise also, earlier two Commissioners went on disposing the cases at a fast speed with Vinod Kumar Tiwari having disposed of 12700 cases with quality judgements elaborately worded in a short span of just 24 months while this figure does not include matters of Show-Cause notices and Non-Compliance matters. It is significant that he even heard some cases on different dates to ensure enough opportunity to respondent public-authorities to defend their case like in his verdict dated 16.01.2025 in petition-number CIC/GNCTD/A/2024/108412 in the matter “Sanjeev Kumar versus Directorate of Health Services (GNCTD”. He even imposed penalty on the PIO and awarded compensation to the petitioner apart from making recommendations while highlighting malpractices in working of private hospitals with DHS being the mute spectator.  Even Delhi High Court dismissed a writ-petition WPC 596/2026 against this verdict on first day of hearing i.e. 16.01.2026. Even present Chief Information Commissioner Raj Kumar Goyal echoed likewise in his verdict dated 16.01.2026 observing that despite 20 years of implementation of the RTI Act, public information officers and first appellate authorities in DHS (GNCTD) were not alert to their legal responsibilities terming it to be a serious issue.

At the same time, Vinod Kumar Tiwari praised such officers who respond to matters nicely not only while responding to RTI applications, but also while presenting their case before the Commission. Example is decision dated 17.11.2025 in file-number CIC/DDATY/A/2024/114518 in the matter “Pawan Jindal versus Delhi Development Authority (DDA)” where he praised Rahul Gupta, PIO-cum-Executive Engineer (DDA) for his nicely presenting the case before the Commission.  Such praise in a CIC-verdict motivates others to do similar nice work to handle RTI matters.

However, RTI rules (and not the RTI Act) need important modifications mainly to prevent misuse of the Act and minimising challenge to CIC verdicts in courts. Notification should be to declare all public-private-partnerships, sports-bodies, cooperative-societies and other such bodies, public-authorities under RTI Act. Land and Building Departments of central and state governments should study all cases of allotment of land or government-accommodations at subsidised rates or lease, and declare all these as public-authorities under RTI Act. For future, land or government-accommodations should be provided at subsidised rates on pre-condition of beneficiaries coming under purview of RTI Act.

Offices like those of President, Prime Minister, Governor, Lt Governor and Chief Minister must not act like “Post Offices” by transferring RTI applications under section 6(3) of RTI Act to concerned departments. These offices should entertain RTI applications pertaining to their respective offices only, and returning rest others to RTI applicants advising applicants to file RTI applications directly to concerned departments.

Considering vast participation of public-money in private sector banks, all private sector banks must be under purview of RTI Act. Already all employees up-to highest post of CMD are public servants according to Banking Regulation Act. Reserve Bank of India (RBI) had to impose restrictions on withdrawal of money for some time on a prominent private sector bank. Former CMD of another prominent private sector Bank is under arrest for serious charges of misappropriation of public-money in the Bank. Inspection Reports of private banks revealed under RTI Act by RBI reveal gross misuse of public money by top management. Another private sector bank is in notoriety for large number of Non-Performing Assets (NPAs). Heavy fluctuation in share-prices of certain private sector banks tend to doubt regarding safety of public money in private sector banks. Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (RBI subsidiary) has to pay maximum rupees five lakhs from state-funds to each depositor of the bank including those in private sector which collapses due to massive irregularities, which is public-funding to declare private sector banks as “public-authorities” under section 2(h) of RTI Act.

Section 27 and 28 of RTI Act give power to Competent Authorities and state-governments to draft their own rules which include fixing of RTI fees. Several Competent Authorities and states misused their power by having RTI fees as high as rupees 500However Supreme Court in its verdict dated 20.03.2018 imposed a capping of rupees fifty to be maximum RTI fees. RTI-fees should be uniformly rupees 50 inclusive of copying-charges of first twenty copied pages Making basic RTI-fees at rupees fifty will largely prevent misuse of RTI Act. There must not be any fees for filing First or Second Appeals.

Handling cost of a postal-order of value rupees ten costs postal-department about rupees fifty with cost of handling of postal-orders by a public-authority and bank-clearing even extra. Postal Department should issue special RTI-stamps (like earlier stamps for licence-fees of radios and TV sets) in denominations of rupees 2, 10 and 50 which will save crores of rupees annually to public-exchequers in using postal-orders as mode of payment of RTI fees.  These RTI stamps should be available at all post-offices and counters of public-authorities and other convenient sale-points. Post-free RTI-applications addressed to central public-authorities should be accepted at all about 160000 post-offices rather than just about 4500 post offices presently. It is not difficult because every post-office however small it may be, daily sends post-bag to Head Post Office with registered post, cash and unsold revenue-articles. This post-bag can carry post-free RTI-applications received at the post-office.

Decision dated 02.11.2012 by Punjab & Haryana High Court in the matter “Fruit and Vegetable Union versus Unknown” (CWP 4787 of 2011) requiring ID proof compulsorily with every RTI application, First Appeal and petitions filed with Information Commissions should be compulsorily adopted throughout the country Police-enquiry conducted at behest of some Indian missions abroad established that a petitioner approached Central Information Commission with name and address both of which did not exist. RTI-responses and orders of First Appellate Authorities should be auto-emailed rather than RTI-applicants required to search portals for viewing of RTI-responses and orders by First Appellate Authorities. Websites designed by National Informatics Centre (NIC) for central public-authorities should be mandatorily for all states. This has become necessary for state like Odisha which has made online filing of RTI-applications a mockery when it is compulsory to download online-filled RTI-application, and then send it by post to concerned department.

Delhi High Court in its order dated 08.08.2018 in WPC 8278 of 2018 in the matter “Anil Dutt Sharma versus Government of NCT Delhi and others” mentioned – This Court is of the prima facie view that the Right-To-Information Act, 2005 would now override the Delhi Right To Information Act, 2001. DRTI Act has lost all with implementation of RTI Act 2005. Very few applications are filed under DRTI Act. All such acts legislated by individual states, before RTI Act 2005 came into existence must be repealed.

text:
The Hypocrites and Protest of 10th Oct
• This is a named political mobilisation (CJP plus Left student unions), not a neighbourhood flash protest. The demand is political: CEC resignation and scrapping SIR.
• It is illegal under the order now in force. Organisers were told no, and have said they will come anyway.
• The same formation’s July march breached the no-march condition, reached near Parliament, and ended in clashes in which police reported stones, bottles and injuries to officers.
• Article 19 is not a right to an unlimited assembly at a banned site. Designated protest sites still run on prior intimation, caps on numbers, and conditions. Jantar Mantar is not a free-fire zone for 50,000 people after a three-day notice. All liberals and pseudo-liberals demanding right to protest is misplaced.
• The disruption — Metro gates, cancelled long-distance trains, closed markets — is the cost of an unauthorised convergence, not evidence that the state is “at war with citizens.”
• Social media scale (CJP’s Instagram following has been reported in the tens of millions) explains coordinated narrative. Funding questions exist and are unanswered; they are not proven.
• the same campus/student political ecosystem that is mobilising for tomorrow’s unauthorised Jantar Mantar protest — Congress-linked and Left student outfits — has no public line tonight on an internal-committee dismissal of their own MP-professor after complaints by 11 students. Complete lack of ideology and real cause.
• Communist one-party states — the USSR, Mao’s China, Cambodia under the Khmer Rouge — killed tens of millions of their own people and banned opposition, a free press and real elections. In a democracy the same current is a small elected fringe, yet it still treats streets, campuses and institutions as instruments to impose its line rather than win a mandate.
• Abhijeet Dipke ran AAP’s social-media and campaign work from 2020 to 2023, then built the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) as a meme page in May 2026. Ashutosh Ranka, a London School of Economics graduate and former McKinsey consultant, worked on AAP media and data, became the party’s Rajasthan Intellectual Wing secretary in December 2025, and donated ₹21,100 to AAP in 2025–26, a sum that appears on the party’s Election Commission list. Saurav Das is an RTI journalist, failed in CLA, who has written for The Caravan, The Wire and Article 14. He was named a CJP spokesperson in June. On 24 September an FIR in Delhi named Dipke, Das, Ranka and Ratna Singh over a morphed image of a woman displayed at their Jantar Mantar protest. That is a police case. AAP’s Sanjay Singh has already said party members will join the 10 October march, while Arvind Kejriwal has amplified the same group for months.
• They have not led a single agitation against AAP’s school record in Delhi or against Congress on the JNU dismissal of their own MP. The demand list is the opposition’s: CEC resignation, scrap SIR, ballot papers. A protest whose organisers come out of AAP, take AAP money and manpower, and never turn the same street pressure on AAP or Congress is a political front, not a natural reaction.
• On 23 September The Indian Express reported that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had put objections on record at least 14 times in 10 months, on Form 6, roll additions and deletions, and access to the voter database. The same day Rahul Gandhi called it “vote chori” and “an act of treason” by the BJP, the RSS and the Election Commission. The next day he demanded Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation and called him a traitor. Congress’s line was that the CEC is “Modi’s puppet.” Kapil Sibal asked for his removal and for elections in that period to be treated as tainted. CJP, Left student unions and AAP are now marching on exactly that demand: Kumar out, SIR scrapped, ballot papers. Sanjay Singh has said AAP members will join a protest CJP is organising. 🗳️ AP LOCAL BODY POLLS | SEC gears up for two-phase election plan
The Andhra Pradesh State Election Commission (SEC) has stepped up preparations for the long-pending rural and urban local body elections, with officials being told to remain ready to begin the poll process at short notice.

State Election Commissioner Anil Chandra Punetha held a three-hour review with district collectors, SPs, police commissioners and senior officials on October 8, directing them to keep manpower, security and election logistics ready once the remaining legal and administrative issues are cleared.

🔹 Two-phase election plan

According to a Times of India report, the SEC has prepared a two-phase strategy aimed at completing the local body election process by December 2026.

The proposed structure reportedly includes:

Phase 1: Elections to 59 Urban Local Bodies

Phase 2: Elections to the remaining urban bodies along with rural local bodies, including thousands of gram panchayats and wards across Andhra Pradesh.

The SEC has already finalised polling-station lists for 59 ULBs, including 58 municipalities/nagar panchayats and the Vizianagaram Municipal Corporation, indicating that a significant portion of the groundwork is complete.

⚖️ BC reservations remain the biggest legal question

The election process is closely linked to the continuing dispute over 34% reservation for Backward Classes in local bodies.

On October 1, the Andhra Pradesh High Court struck down the government orders providing 34% BC reservation, holding that the combined SC, ST and BC reservation crossed the 50% ceiling without the required empirical exercise. The court also directed the government and SEC to move ahead with the election process within six weeks.

The matter has since reached the Supreme Court, where related petitions are being considered.

Until there is greater legal clarity on reservations, final seat-wise reservation and candidate calculations remain a key unresolved factor.

💰 Why the elections are financially important

The elections are not only politically significant.

The Andhra Pradesh government has said that delays could affect access to Finance Commission grants for local bodies.

Earlier cabinet-level discussions identified around ₹3,862 crore in 16th Finance Commission-linked grants — including approximately ₹2,300 crore for rural local bodies and ₹1,562 crore for urban bodies — as funds that could be affected if elected bodies are not constituted in time.

That makes the poll calendar important not just for political representation, but also for local infrastructure and municipal finances.

🏛️ Political parties already preparing

The ruling NDA alliance has simultaneously intensified its political preparations.

Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu and Deputy Chief Minister Pawan Kalyan recently held discussions on seat-sharing, candidate selection and coordination between TDP and Jana Sena ahead of the polls.

TDP leaders have also said that multiple rounds of seat-sharing discussions have already taken place, though final allocations remain linked to the reservation matrix.

🔎 What happens next?

The election machinery appears increasingly ready.

The real triggers now are:

• final legal clarity on BC reservations
• formal SEC notification
• finalisation of reservation rosters
• candidate selection and alliance seat-sharing
• deployment of election personnel and security

Once those pieces fall into place, Andhra Pradesh could move quickly into one of its largest grassroots electoral exercises in recent years.

The key issue now is no longer whether the SEC is preparing.

The bigger question is: when will the legal and reservation hurdles clear sufficiently for the election schedule to be officially announced?

My friend’s younger sister disappeared from their family house in Port Harcourt three years ago. The police closed the case after six months and said she had probably run away.
Last month the sister’s old Facebook account, which the family had memorialized, began liking photos the girl had never seen. The likes always arrived between 1 and 2 a.m. and only on pictures that showed the front gate of the house.
Two nights ago the girl’s mother received a voice note from the account. It was her daughter’s voice, quiet and close to the microphone, saying the padlock on the gate was the wrong one and that she had been standing outside every evening waiting for someone to notice the new chain.
This morning the family found the original padlock lying on the veranda, cut clean through, and a second, heavier chain already fastened in its place. No one in the house remembers buying it. The voice note is still on the phone, and it ends with the sound of someone breathing just on the other side of the gate.

text:
Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.
